prompt: On an Android phone, what does a React Native `<Text>` become?

choices.text:
A `

` element inside a WebView the app hides
choices.why: There is no WebView: nothing in a React Native app draws HTML.

choices.text: Kotlin source that the build generates from the component

choices.text: A `TextView`

prompt: A component runs a loop that takes two seconds. What does the person holding the phone notice?

choices.text: Scrolling still works, but presses get no answer until the loop ends
choices.why: Right: native scrolling lives on the main thread, and every answer you wrote waits for the JavaScript thread.

choices.text: The whole app freezes, scrolling included, and Android offers to close it
choices.why: That is the main thread blocked. The loop blocks the JavaScript thread, which is a different one.

choices.text: Nothing, because Hermes moves long loops to a background thread
choices.why: Hermes runs your code on one thread and moves nothing.

choices.text: The app restarts
choices.why: A slow loop is not a crash.

prompt: Match each step of putting a component on screen with where it happens.

pairs.left: layout: flexbox becomes sizes and positions
mount: native views are created or updated

prompt: Which thread may create or change a native view?

choices.text: Any thread, as long as it holds a reference to the view
choices.why: Both platforms refuse view changes from other threads.

choices.text: The JavaScript thread
choices.why: That is where React decides what changes; it hands the result over.

choices.text: Yoga's thread
choices.why: Yoga computes sizes and positions; it owns no thread and touches no view.

choices.text: The main thread
choices.why: Right, and that is why a native module that draws hands its work to it.

prompt: Under the old bridge, why could JavaScript not ask native code for a view's size and use it in the next line?

choices.text: Views had no size until the app was restarted
choices.why: They had one; the problem was getting it back.

choices.text: Every call was a queued message, and the answer arrived later in a callback
choices.why: Right: the bridge was asynchronous by design.

choices.text: Measuring was forbidden on Android
choices.why: Both platforms measure views all the time.

choices.text: JSON cannot represent a number
choices.why: It can; the delay came from the queue, not the format.

prompt: Which of these were costs of the old bridge? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: Data crossing it was serialised to JSON and copied
choices.why: Yes: a large array crossed as text.

choices.text: Every native module was created when the app opened
choices.why: Yes: the bridge needed its table of modules up front.

choices.text: Components had to be written in Objective-C
choices.why: Components were JavaScript then as now.

choices.text: A JavaScript-driven animation stuttered when the JavaScript thread was busy
choices.why: Yes: each frame was a message too.

prompt: A 2021 blog post advises sending fewer, larger messages "to reduce bridge traffic". What should you conclude for an app on React Native 0.88?

choices.text: Follow it exactly: the bridge is still there, just renamed
choices.why: There is no bridge in 0.88; JSI calls are not queued messages.

choices.text: Its mechanism no longer exists; keep only the part about not blocking the JavaScript thread
choices.why: Right: the bridge is gone, and the thread it ran on is still one thread.

choices.text: Ignore everything written before 2024 about React Native
choices.why: Components and hooks are written as they were; most of it still applies.

choices.text: Turn the bridge back on for the screens that send lots of data
choices.why: Since 0.82 the old architecture cannot be turned on at all.

prompt: Match each part of the new architecture with what it does.

pairs.right: lets JavaScript call a C++ object directly
keeps the tree of views and mounts native views
native modules created on first use
writes the glue from a typed spec at build time

right_distractors: serialises calls to JSON in batches

prompt: A native module's `getString()` is called through JSI and does 300 ms of disk work before returning. What happens?

choices.text: Hermes refuses the call because it is too slow
choices.why: Nothing measures or refuses it.

choices.text: Nothing waits, because JSI moves synchronous calls to a background queue
choices.why: JSI calls the function directly on the calling thread; it queues nothing.

choices.text: The main thread waits, and the screen freezes
choices.why: The call runs on the JavaScript thread, not the main one.

choices.text: The JavaScript thread waits the 300 ms
choices.why: Right: a synchronous call removes the overhead of crossing, not the cost of the work.

prompt: An app has forty libraries installed and its first screen uses three native modules. With TurboModules, which are created at launch?

choices.text: The three the first screen calls
choices.why: Right: each is created the first time JavaScript asks for it.

choices.text: All forty, so that any of them can be called
choices.why: That was the bridge's table. TurboModules wait to be asked for.

choices.text: None until the user grants a permission
choices.why: Permissions have nothing to do with when modules are created.

choices.text: Only the ones written in C++
choices.why: The language a module is written in does not decide when it is created.

choices.text: Only on iOS, where the bridge is still the default

choices.text: Opening the app's web build in a browser

prompt: `npm install` fails behind your office network with a certificate error. Which fix is the right one?

choices.text: Turn off strict SSL in npm's settings
choices.why: That makes every download accept anybody's answer, for good.

choices.text: Run npm with `sudo`
choices.why: Root trusts the same certificates you do; it only creates permission problems.

choices.text: Install an older Node.js that does not check certificates
choices.why: Every Node.js checks them, and an old one brings its own problems.

choices.text: Ask its administrators for their CA file and point `NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS` at it
choices.why: Right: Node.js then trusts that one certificate and still checks everything.
